  **Impact:** Keeps him on injured reserve without counting against the 90-man roster.

- **Raiders waived DL Brodric Martin with an injury designation, prior to cut to 53.**  
  **Impact:** Clears a path on the roster; his injury status is the key context.

- **Chargers waived LS Peter Bowden with no recall.**  
  **Impact:** Los Angeles moves on from a special teams depth option.

- **Colts waived Jack Wilson with an injury settlement.**  
  **Impact:** Ends the team’s commitment after the injury-related move.

fantasypoints.summary:
- **Jaxon Smith-Njigba** — Heavy usage in 2-WR or lighter sets drove his breakout; those snaps produced 51% of his receiving yards and 48% of his fantasy points, so scheme can fully support elite WR1 production. Ryan Heath [2]
- **Ladd McConkey** — His 2025 route profile was almost all in heavier personnel, and Ryan Heath thinks he’s the best bet to become this year’s Jaxon Smith-Njigba. Ryan Heath [2]
- **Drake London** — He was elite on plays with 2 or fewer WRs, making him a dark-horse candidate to lead all receivers in fantasy points. Ryan Heath [2]
- **Christian Watson** — He looks locked into a full-time route share in Green Bay, giving him fringe-WR1 upside if the usage holds. Ryan Heath [2]
- **Mike Evans** — His production spikes in heavier personnel, and if healthy he’s a strong bounce-back fantasy candidate. Ryan Heath [2]
- **Colston Loveland** — The Bears’ 3-TE sets unlocked massive efficiency, and Ryan Heath thinks he can lead Chicago in receiving and join the position’s top tier. Ryan Heath [2]
- **Sam LaPorta** — His multi-TE-set production has been elite enough that his early ADP looks mispriced. Ryan Heath [2]
- **Jadarian Price** — Seattle appears ready to hand him the backfield after Kenneth Walker’s departure, putting him on the fantasy radar immediately. Tom Brolley [1]
- **Kenneth Walker** — He’s moved on to Kansas City, leaving Seattle’s backfield and opening the door for Price. Tom Brolley [1]

CIN.summary:
- **Bengals schedule** — Cincinnati’s 2026 slate has several early measuring-stick games, with Week 2 at Houston, Week 4 vs. Jacksonville, Week 3 at Pittsburgh, and a Week 11 trip to Washington highlighted as especially important. The piece frames those matchups as key indicators of whether the Bengals can contend the way they did in 2021 and 2022. [2]

- **Joe Burrow** — The Bengals open the season at home against Tampa Bay, giving Burrow an early chance to face Baker Mayfield again in a rare No. 1-pick quarterback matchup. Burrow has not beaten Mayfield yet, and the game also sets the tone for Cincinnati’s home schedule. [6]

- **Zac Taylor** — Cincinnati will not get a bye immediately after its Spain trip; instead, it is slated for back-to-back primetime games in Weeks 10 and 11 after Madrid. That means the post-international stretch is more demanding than a recovery week, with Pittsburgh at home on Sunday night and Washington on the road on Monday night. [7]

- **Defensive back room** — Cornerback depth is still an issue, even after the Bengals drafted Tacario Davis in the third round. The article says Davis’s size could push Dax Hill back inside to nickel, with DJ Ivey, Jalen Davis, and Josh Newton next up if there’s an injury. [5]

- **Orlando Brown Jr.** — Brown publicly endorsed Cincinnati’s trade for Dexter Lawrence, saying Lawrence is a great fit for what the Bengals are. The move cost Cincinnati the No. 10 pick, and Brown’s reaction underscores how aggressively the team is leaning into an “all-in” roster build. [8]

GB.summary:
- **Matt LaFleur / Packers schedule** — Green Bay’s leaked opening slate looks favorable: at Minnesota in Week 1, then three straight out-of-division opponents, with none of the first four opponents having made the playoffs last season. If the leaks hold, that gives the Packers a softer runway while they wait for Micah Parsons’ return. [2]

- **Green Bay Packers** — The Packers are reportedly set for six primetime games in 2026, with five at Lambeau Field, which would be the most in franchise history. That’s a major stage for a team trying to push back into NFC North contention, and it adds a lot of fantasy-friendly showcase spots. [5]

- **Green Bay Packers** — Green Bay is also being linked to a Christmas Day game against the Bears, with a Week 5 Lambeau meeting and a Christmas road trip to Chicago both mentioned in the leak reporting. If accurate, that would give the Packers two high-profile division games against a key rival, with Parsons’ availability a potential swing factor. [2, 7]

- **Green Bay Packers** — The Packers got a Week 11 bye, which is better than last year’s Week 5 bye, but they also face negative rest differential in three of six NFC North games, including both matchups with a “chief contender” in the division. That could matter late in the season when divisional tiebreakers and injury recovery become more important. [8]

- **Luke Lachey** — Green Bay was awarded the former Iowa tight end off waivers from Houston, and the article frames him as a potential answer to the Packers’ need for a blocking tight end. He was a 2025 seventh-round pick who spent all of last season on the Texans’ practice squad, so this is a low-cost depth addition with a clear role to fight for. [6]

- **M.J. Devonshire** — The Packers also claimed the cornerback off waivers from Buffalo, giving them a full 90-man roster heading into OTAs. The item does not specify his role outlook, but he’s now in the mix as Green Bay fills out depth. [6]

PHI.summary:
- **Jalen Hurts** — He’s being framed as entering a “prove-it” season after Philadelphia’s passing game ranked in the bottom third of the league in back-to-back seasons. NFL personnel evaluators still vary on his standing, but the spotlight is clearly on what he does next. What to watch: whether the offense’s shift to more play-action and under-center work helps him take a step forward. [4, 8]

- **Sean Mannion** — The Eagles are introducing a new offensive scheme under Mannion, and the home crowd will get its first look at it early in the season. The change comes after the offense’s recent struggles, so implementation matters as much as design. The key next question is how smoothly Hurts adapts to the added play-action and under-center emphasis. [3, 8]

- **A.J. Brown / DeVonta Smith / Elijah Moore** — Philadelphia’s passing game is being reshaped around a likely Brown departure, with Smith described as the new No. 1 and Moore also working with Hurts this offseason. Berman’s note also says the Eagles will miss Brown early in the season. That makes Smith’s role more important and gives Moore a path to relevance if the target tree thins as expected. [3, 4]

- **Julian Neal (CB)** — Seattle used a third-round pick on Neal after losing Riq Woolen this offseason and adding depth pieces like Josh Jobe, Noah Igbinoghene and Shemar Jean-Charles. The piece says Neal doesn’t arrive with immediate starter expectations, but his size, length, physicality and contact willingness are a clear fit for the secondary’s direction. What to watch next: how quickly he closes the gap in a cornerback room that still lacks a true identity shift. [3]
